newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - July 11.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - July 11.

text.p: This daily press summary is produced for Reuters by the Broadcast Monitoring Company, which is responsible for its contents. DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- CO-FOUNDER OF APPLE IN LINE FOR TOP POST

Steve Jobs, the co-founder of Apple Computer who was ousted in 1985 then reinstated last year, has been tipped as the likely successor to chairman and chief executive Gil Amelio who resigned on Wednesday. Macintosh computers chief financial officer Fred Anderson would not rule out Jobs as a candidate, but stressed the company was looking for external recruits at the moment. (Daily Telegraph p. 34)
-- ATOMIC SALE PROCEEDS GO TOWARDS PAYING DEBT

The Atomic Energy Authority has revealed in its latest report and accounts that over 60 per cent (141m stg) of the funds it raised from the 1996 220m stg privatisation of AEA Technology has been used to clear the firm's remaining public sector debts. The write-off was administered by the Conservative government in 1996, as former prime minister John Major believed the business could not fund its debt. The authority continues to receive government aid, reportedly receiving 143m stg in the year to March 30th.
-- ROBERT LOWE GETS FIT FOR WORLD CUP

Football strips to cardboard box group Robert Lowe unveiled an 83 per cent increase in full year profits on Thursday to 1.65m stg. Declining profits from sportswear following the European Championships were offset by growth on RL's packaging side and the 6.5m stg acquisition of Westfield Medical. Company chairman Robert Sebire is now preparing for business from World Cup 1998 expecting to supply kits for several of the competing countries.
THE TIMES
-- MORTGAGES POISED TO RISE AGAIN AS WORRIED BANK PUTS UP INTEREST RATES

Millions of homeowners are facing the prospect of increased mortgage costs after the Bank of England increased interest rates for the third consecutive month yesterday. Chancellor Gordon Brown defended the measures as necessary for an economy "in danger of becoming seriously out of balance" because of mistakes made by the previous government.
-- CWS SCANDAL CLAIMS THREE AT HAMBROS

Three senior figures at merchant bank Hambros have been forced to leave the firm after it was revealed they were involved in the Co-operative Wholesale Society scandal. Nigel Pantling, head of corporate finance at Hambros, and two directors of the bank, left after an investigation by City solicitor Norton Rose found that Hambros had used confidential CWS documents while working on an aborted 1.2bn stg bid for CWS for Andrew Regan's Galileo.
-- IMPROVED SALES RESTORE CONFIDENCE IN STOREHOUSE

Storehouse, the retail group which owns the Mothercare and BhS chains, has announced better-than-expected sales for the first quarter of this year. The group reported a 14.5 per cent increase in total sales, with analysts estimating the like-for- like increase in sales at BhS at 2.5 per cent and 3 per cent at Mothercare.
THE GUARDIAN
-- LAW FEES EAT UP MAXWELL LEGACY

The High Court has heard that all but 60,000 pounds stg of the 1.68m stg personal fortune of the late Robert Maxwell could be swallowed up in fees. Accountancy firm Buchler Phillips, receivers to the late tycoon's estate, have submitted a bill for 1,628,572 pounds stg to cover fees and costs for the recovery of assets worth 1,672,500 pound stg.
-- SHAREHOLDERS BACK TUNNEL RESCUE MOVE

Shareholders in Eurotunnel, the operator of the Channel Tunnel, have voted to support a last-ditch rescue plan for the troubled company. The decision to authorise a FFr70bn (7bn stg) debt restructuring deal was made at an extraordinary general meeting in Paris on Thursday.
-- DRINKS MERGER CLOSER

French luxury goods group LVMH is expected next week to submit formal proposals for a merger of its Moet Hennessy drinks division with those of Guinness and Grand Metropolitan. Agreement on the three-way tie-up could see LVMH remove its opposition to the proposed 24bn stg mega-merger of Guinness and GrandMet.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- BECKETT SET TO RULE OUT UTILITY PROFIT-SHARING

A review of utility regulation which was launched last week by Trade Secretary Margaret Beckett seems certain to rule that an annual profit-sharing mechanism, designed to cream off excess company profits, would be too bureaucratic to operate in practice. Such a conclusion would reverse a key government policy proposal intended to reform the privatised utilities.
-- 50M STG JARVIS RAIL DEAL UNDER FIRE

There have been calls for a Monopolies and Mergers Commission inquiry into the 55m stg deal under which Jarvis, the Essex construction group, will buy two privatised railway track renewals companies. Rival firms have criticised the deal on competition grounds, arguing that the consolidation would restrict the leasing market for heavy plant and machinery.
-- COMPAQ ADDS TO PRICE WAR FEARS AFTER APPLE CHIEF GOES

Compaq Computer, the largest manufacturer of PCs in North America, has announced price cuts of up to 22 per cent on many of its PCs for corporate customers. The move, which could herald a new price cutting war in the sector, came just one day after Hewlett-Packard cut prices by up to 24 per cent. A price war could prove disastrous for Apple Computer, which saw its chief executive Gil Amelio ousted on Wednesday night.
